title: U.S. Army detonates toxic material in Iowa amid health, environmental concerns
byline: Ty Oneil; John Seewer; Scott Bauer
html:
The U.S. Army detonates a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday.Jim Urquhart/Reuters

The U.S. Army intentionally blew up the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday after officials said the degraded materials were at risk of exploding uncontrollably as temperatures cooled.

Video footage from several miles away showed two white plumes rolling over the detonation site before the clouds quickly dissipated. Journalists reported hearing a loud boom at the same time. Despite warnings to stay inside, some residents pulled to the side of a road to watch the blast upwind from the ammunition plant.

Environmentalists voiced concerns about possible health and environmental effects from the controlled detonation of the bomb-making chemicals at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. But officials warned about the dangers of waiting too long, and a court ultimately cleared the way for the military to carry out the blast.

Officials advised people nearby to be ready to evacuate to avoid toxic dust in the air but also sought to assure them that barriers around the blast zone should limit much of the plume.

Some residents near Middletown sealed their windows and doors as a precaution to keep out any lead dust that may result from the detonation. Others who live farther away had raised concerns about the possible paths the plume could take depending on the wind.

The Army set up blast barriers around the bunkers where the 5 tons of lead azide was detonated and used ballistic gels and foams to absorb the lead dust. It said beforehand that it also would douse the materials with thousands of gallons of water.

Administration building at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Tuesday.Austin Johnson/The Associated Press
summary: Video footage from several miles away showed two white plumes rolling over the detonation site before the clouds quickly dissipated
